questions.question: What is Apache Maven and what is 'convention over configuration'?
questions.title: What Is Maven?
questions.direct_answer: Apache Maven is a project build and dependency-management tool centered on a POM, standard lifecycles, plugins, and repository coordinates. 'Convention over configuration' means defaults such as `src/main/java`, `src/test/java`, and standard packaging bindings work with little POM configuration; projects can still override those conventions when needed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Maven's design philosophy and can explain 'convention over configuration' — a core concept that appears in Spring Boot and modern Java frameworks
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing Maven only as 'it manages dependencies' without mentioning the full build lifecycle or the convention principle that makes it different from Ant
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast Maven's opinionated conventions with Gradle's flexibility and explain when each approach is better — Maven for standard projects, Gradle when you need custom build logic

sections.title: Maven's Build Automation Philosophy
sections.content:
Apache Maven is a comprehensive build automation tool that manages the entire lifecycle of Java projects — from compiling source code to running tests to packaging deployable artifacts. Think of Maven like an assembly line in a car factory: every car goes through the same stations in the same order (welding, painting, assembly), and you don't need to design the process from scratch each time.

The **convention over configuration** principle means Maven provides sensible defaults for everything — your source code goes in src/main/java, tests in src/test/java, and built artifacts in target/. Instead of writing hundreds of lines of build scripts, you declare what your project needs in a single pom.xml file and Maven figures out the how. This dramatically reduces boilerplate and makes conventional Maven projects immediately familiar to any Java developer. Maven executes a **build lifecycle** with predefined phases: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, and deploy.

sections.title: Maven at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Convention|~Standard layout|src/main/java|no custom scripts|every project looks alike
blue|Lifecycle|~Phases in order|validate to deploy|one command runs all|predictable builds
emerald|Dependencies|~Declarative|pom.xml coordinates|transitive resolution|from Maven Central
violet|Plugins|~Do the real work|compiler, surefire|spring-boot plugin|extend the lifecycle

sections.title: Minimal Maven Project Structure and pom.xml
sections.content:
```text
order-service/
├── pom.xml
└── src/
    ├── main/
    │   ├── java/
    │   └── resources/
    └── test/
        ├── java/
        └── resources/

# With conventional jar packaging:
mvn test
mvn package
```

Maven's defaults know these directories and bind standard compiler, test, and JAR plugin goals. The POM still declares coordinates and any dependencies or non-default behavior.

sections.title: When Maven's Conventions Shine
sections.content:
Use Maven when your project follows standard Java patterns and you want zero-configuration builds. **Enterprise Spring Boot applications** benefit enormously because Maven's conventions align perfectly with Spring's structure — no custom scripting needed for multi-module microservices. **Open-source libraries** almost always use Maven because publishing to Maven Central requires a pom.xml, and the ecosystem expects it. **Teams with junior developers** benefit from Maven's guardrails — there's one obvious way to do things, which prevents fragmentation.

Use Gradle instead when you need complex custom build logic, Android development, or polyglot projects mixing Java with Kotlin or Scala where Gradle's Groovy DSL provides more flexibility.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating Maven as just a dependency downloader**: Freshers often think Maven only fetches JARs from the internet and miss that it orchestrates the entire build lifecycle including compilation, testing, and packaging. This leads to confusion when mvn install does more than expected.
- **Fighting Maven's conventions unnecessarily**: New developers sometimes create custom src/code or src/classes directories instead of using src/main/java, then spend hours configuring Maven to recognize them. Follow the conventions — they exist for good reasons and every IDE understands them.
- **Not understanding the parent POM hierarchy**: Freshers declare spring-boot-starter-parent as a dependency instead of a parent, which breaks version management and plugin inheritance, causing cryptic build errors.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Convention over configuration**: Maven defines standard project layouts and build phases so you don't write custom scripts — just declare dependencies and goals
- **Build lifecycle**: Maven executes phases in order (clean → validate → compile → test → package → install → deploy) with each phase having pre-defined behavior
- **Declarative configuration**: The pom.xml file describes what your project is and what it needs — Maven figures out how to build it
- **Dependency management**: Maven automatically downloads libraries from Maven Central and resolves transitive dependencies without manual intervention
- **Plugin ecosystem**: Maven's functionality comes from plugins (compiler, surefire for tests, jar packager) that execute during lifecycle phases

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Maven is a build automation tool for Java that manages dependencies and executes the full build lifecycle from compiling code to packaging deployable artifacts. The key idea is convention over configuration — Maven gives you standard directory layouts and build phases so you don't write custom scripts. For example, your Java source always goes in src slash main slash java and tests in src slash test slash java. When you run mvn package, Maven automatically compiles your code, runs tests, and creates a JAR file without you configuring those steps explicitly. This is different from older tools like Ant where you'd write hundreds of lines of XML to define every compilation step. In a Spring Boot project, you just declare spring-boot-starter-web in your pom dot XML, and Maven downloads not just that library but also all its transitive dependencies like Tomcat and Jackson. The convention approach means conventional Maven projects looks the same, which is huge for team productivity. One common mistake freshers make is treating Maven as just a dependency downloader — it's actually orchestrating your entire build process. If you need lots of custom build logic or non-Java languages, you might choose Gradle instead, but for standard Java backend work, Maven's conventions eliminate a ton of boilerplate.

questions.question: What are Maven coordinates and what do groupId, artifactId, and version mean?
questions.title: Maven Coordinates: groupId, artifactId, version (GAV)
questions.direct_answer: Maven identifies a dependency with coordinates. The common form is `groupId:artifactId:version`; complete coordinates can also include type and classifier, which distinguish variants such as a test JAR. `groupId` names the publishing namespace, `artifactId` names the module, and `version` selects a release. Maven version strings are not required to follow Semantic Versioning.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Maven fluency — GAV coordinates appear in every pom.xml dependency declaration and are essential for dependency resolution
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing groupId with package name or not understanding that groupId prevents naming collisions between different organizations
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Maven coordinates solve the namespace collision problem — two organizations can publish artifacts with the same artifactId as long as their groupIds differ, like com.google.guava:guava vs com.github.ben-manes.caffeine:caffeine

sections.title: Maven's Universal Artifact Addressing System
sections.content:
Maven coordinates (also called **GAV coordinates** for groupId, artifactId, version) are the unique address for any library or module in the Maven ecosystem. Think of them like a postal address: the **groupId** is the country and city (organization namespace), the **artifactId** is the street and house number (specific project), and the **version** is the apartment number (release).

For example, org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web:3.2.0 uniquely identifies one specific JAR file among millions. The groupId follows reverse-domain naming like com.company.product to ensure global uniqueness — your company owns that namespace just like it owns the domain. The artifactId names the specific module within that organization, like user-service or payment-api. The version follows semantic versioning conventions (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) to signal compatibility. Maven uses these coordinates to locate artifacts in repositories, resolve dependencies, and avoid naming conflicts. When you declare a dependency, Maven searches repositories using the coordinate path: groupId becomes directories, artifactId is the folder, version is the subfolder.

sections.title: GAV Coordinates
sections.content:
amber|groupId|~Organization namespace|reverse domain|org.springframework|prevents collisions
blue|artifactId|~Module name|spring-core|becomes the JAR name|unique within group
emerald|version|~Release number|MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH|1.0.0 or 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT|semantic versioning
violet|Maps to a path|~Repo lookup|group becomes folders|then artifact, then version|artifact-version.jar

sections.title: Declaring Dependencies with Maven Coordinates
sections.content:
```xml
// pom.xml dependency section showing GAV coordinates
<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>  // Organization namespace
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>  // Specific module
    <version>3.2.0</version>  // Release version
  </dependency>
  
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
    <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
    <version>8.2.0</version>
    <scope>runtime</scope>  // Only needed at runtime, not compile time
  </dependency>
  
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
    <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
    <version>1.18.30</version>
    <scope>provided</scope>  // Compile-time only, not packaged
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

// These coordinates map to repository paths:
// org/springframework/boot/spring-boot-starter-data-jpa/3.2.0/spring-boot-starter-data-jpa-3.2.0.jar
```

sections.title: When Maven Coordinates Matter Most
sections.content: You interact with Maven coordinates every time you add a library to your project — searching search.maven.org or mvnrepository.com for the right GAV. **Multi-module projects** use coordinates to reference sibling modules: if order-service depends on common-utils, you declare com.company:common-utils:1.0.0 as a dependency. **Publishing your own library** requires choosing coordinates carefully — the groupId must match a domain you control (verified when publishing to Maven Central), and the artifactId should clearly identify the module's purpose. **Dependency version management** relies on coordinates: Spring Boot's parent POM defines versions for hundreds of artifacts by their groupId and artifactId, letting you omit version numbers in your dependencies. Understanding coordinates is critical when resolving **version conflicts** — Maven uses the nearest definition rule based on dependency tree depth.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using arbitrary groupId values**: Freshers often invent groupIds like my.project or test.app instead of reverse-domain names. This causes publication rejections and namespace collisions. Always use a domain you control: com.yourcompany or io.github.yourusername.
- **Confusing groupId with Java package names**: The groupId doesn't have to match your code's package structure. groupId is an organizational namespace for Maven artifacts, while packages organize Java classes. They often align by convention (org.springframework groupId with org.springframework.boot packages), but it's not required.
- **Forgetting that artifactId should be globally unique within groupId**: Two modules in your organization can't have the same artifactId even if they're in different Git repos — the groupId plus artifactId must uniquely identify the module across all your projects.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **GAV coordinates**: groupId, artifactId, and version together form a unique identifier for every Maven artifact worldwide
- **groupId namespace**: Uses reverse-domain notation (com.company.product) to ensure global uniqueness and prevent naming collisions between organizations
- **artifactId specificity**: Names the specific module or library within the groupId namespace, like spring-core or user-service
- **version semantics**: Follows MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH format where major changes break compatibility, minor adds features, patch fixes bugs
- **Repository paths**: Coordinates map directly to filesystem paths in Maven repositories: groupId/artifactId/version/artifactId-version.jar

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Maven coordinates are the unique identifier for any library or module in the Maven world. They're written as three parts: groupId colon artifactId colon version, like org dot springframework dot boot colon spring-boot-starter-web colon 3.2.0. The groupId is the organization namespace using reverse-domain format — it's like the publisher of the library. For example, org dot springframework means it's published by the Spring team. The artifactId is the specific module name within that organization, so spring-boot-starter-web is one particular library they publish. The version selects the artifact version using the producer's versioning scheme. When you add a dependency to your pom dot XML, you specify these three pieces and Maven uses them to find and download the right JAR file. The coordinates solve a critical problem: two different companies could both have a library called utils, but com dot google colon utils and com dot company colon utils are completely different artifacts that won't collide. Maven converts coordinates into file paths — the groupId becomes nested directories, then artifactId, then version. One mistake freshers make is using random groupIds like my dot project instead of proper reverse-domain names. When you publish to Maven Central, you have to prove you own that domain, so always use something like io dot github dot yourusername if you don't have a company domain.

questions.question: What is the difference between a SNAPSHOT version and a release version in Maven?
questions.title: SNAPSHOT vs Release Versions in Maven
questions.direct_answer: A `-SNAPSHOT` version identifies a changing development line, so a repository may publish newer timestamped builds under the same base version and Maven checks according to repository update policy. A release version such as `1.0.0` is expected to be immutable and is normally cached. Release naming improves repeatability, but it does not by itself guarantee byte-for-byte reproducible builds.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding Maven versioning semantics — SNAPSHOT behavior is a frequent source of confusion and build reproducibility issues
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that Maven re-downloads SNAPSHOTs periodically or that release versions are cached forever and never checked for updates
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that production deployments must never use SNAPSHOT dependencies because they're non-reproducible — today's 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT could be different code tomorrow

sections.title: Maven's Two Versioning Models
sections.content:
A version ending in **`-SNAPSHOT`** represents ongoing development. A remote repository can contain newer timestamped snapshot builds for the same base version, and Maven decides when to check using the repository's update policy. The default policy is often daily, but settings and repository definitions can change it; `-U` requests a check for updated snapshots and missing releases.

A **release version** such as `1.0.0` is expected to identify stable, unchanged repository content. Maven normally reuses the cached release unless policy or local state requires another resolution. Repository managers can be configured badly enough to replace releases, so immutability is a publishing rule and repository policy, not magic enforced by the version string alone.

Using releases removes the moving-version problem, but a byte-for-byte reproducible build also needs controlled plugins, JDK/toolchain, operating-system inputs, timestamps, environment, and repository contents.

sections.title: SNAPSHOT vs Release
sections.content:
amber|SNAPSHOT|~Work in progress|1.0.0-SNAPSHOT|can change anytime|re-checked on build
blue|Release|~published as a stable version|1.0.0|immutable bytecode|normally reused from the local repository
emerald|Update policy|~-U forces refresh|daily check by default|cached after first fetch|speed comes from cache
rose|Production rule|~Releases only|reproducible builds|no overnight surprises|never ship SNAPSHOTs

sections.title: Declaring SNAPSHOT vs Release Versions
sections.content:
```xml
<!-- development build: re-fetched as it keeps changing -->
<version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>

<!-- release build: expected to remain immutable once published -->
<version>1.0.0</version>
```
`mvn install -U` forces Maven to re-download the latest SNAPSHOT instead of using the cached copy.

sections.title: SNAPSHOT vs Release Version Behavior
sections.content:
| Aspect | SNAPSHOT Version | Release Version |
|---|---|---|
| Mutability | Changes frequently with new commits | expected to remain immutable once published |
| Maven update check | Re-checks repository daily or on demand | Normally uses the cached release; policy and local state still matter |
| Intended use | Active development and team integration | Production deployments and stable APIs |
| Reproducibility | Non-reproducible — same version different code | Stable coordinate; full reproducibility needs controlled inputs |
| Publishing | Can overwrite existing SNAPSHOT repeatedly | Repositories should reject or prevent replacing the release |

sections.title: When to Use Each Version Type
sections.content: Use **SNAPSHOT versions** during active development when you're building features and need the latest code from your team. If you're working on a multi-module microservices project, the order-service module depends on common-utils:1.0.0-SNAPSHOT so it automatically picks up the latest shared code without constantly bumping version numbers. When you run `mvn install` places the snapshot in the local repository; `mvn deploy` publishes to the configured remote, and teammates get updates on their next build. Switch to **release versions** when you're ready to deploy to production or publish a stable API. Change 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT to 1.0.0, run mvn deploy, then immediately bump to 1.0.1-SNAPSHOT for the next development cycle. Release versions helps a deployment refer to an approved stable artifact — no surprises from overnight commits. Production policies normally avoid mutable SNAPSHOT coordinates because the same coordinate can resolve to changed content.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Deploying SNAPSHOT dependencies to production**: Freshers sometimes ship applications that depend on SNAPSHOT versions, creating a nightmare scenario where production behavior changes unpredictably because Maven silently pulls a newer snapshot with breaking changes. production builds should normally use immutable release coordinates.
- **Not understanding Maven's SNAPSHOT update policy**: By default Maven checks for new SNAPSHOTs once per day, so freshers are confused when their build doesn't pick up the latest code their teammate just pushed. You need mvn clean install -U (uppercase U) to force an immediate update.
- **Reusing release version numbers**: After publishing 1.0.0 to Maven Central, freshers try to republish the same version with bug fixes. Maven Central rejects this because release versions are immutable. You must increment to 1.0.1 for any code change.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **SNAPSHOT:** changing development version; newer builds can appear under one base version.
- **Release:** expected to be immutable and normally cached.
- **Update checks:** controlled by repository policy; `-U` forces an update check.
- **Production:** prefer approved releases, but decide through delivery policy.
- **Reproducibility:** release versions help; toolchains and all other inputs still matter.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A SNAPSHOT such as `1.0.0-SNAPSHOT` is a moving development version. A repository may publish newer timestamped builds under that base version, and Maven checks for updates according to repository policy. A release such as `1.0.0` is expected to stay unchanged and is normally reused from the local repository.

For example, two developers resolving the same SNAPSHOT on different days may receive different builds. Releasing `1.0.0` removes that moving coordinate, but I would not call the build automatically reproducible: the JDK, plugins, environment, repository contents, generated timestamps, and other inputs also affect output. Teams usually keep SNAPSHOTs in development flows and deploy approved releases or immutable artifacts according to their release policy.

questions.question: What is the standard Maven project directory structure?
questions.title: Maven Standard Directory Structure
questions.direct_answer: Maven's standard layout places production Java in `src/main/java`, production resources in `src/main/resources`, tests in `src/test/java`, test resources in `src/test/resources`, and generated build output in `target`. These are defaults, not language rules; a POM can configure alternatives.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Maven project navigation — knowing where to put code, tests, and resources is fundamental for any Java backend work
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing where to put application.properties or other config files — they go in src/main/resources, not in the java directory
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Spring Initializr generates this structure automatically and that target/ is in .gitignore because it's generated output, not source code

sections.title: Maven's Convention-Based Project Layout
sections.content:
Maven uses a standard directory layout so its plugins can find sources and resources without repeated configuration. Production Java normally lives in `src/main/java`, classpath resources in `src/main/resources`, test Java in `src/test/java`, and test-only resources in `src/test/resources`. Maven writes build output under `target`.

The layout is a Maven convention rather than a Java or Spring requirement. A project can configure different source and resource directories, although following the convention usually makes the build easier for tools and teammates to understand. Not every configuration file belongs in resources: only files that must become classpath resources should go there.

In a multi-module build, each child module can have its own POM and standard source tree. Generated output is normally excluded from source control, while source, POMs, and intentionally versioned resources are committed.

sections.title: Standard Maven Layout
sections.content:
amber|src/main/java|~Production code|by package|your application|compiled to target/classes
blue|src/main/resources|~Config + assets|application.properties|static files, SQL|packaged into the JAR
emerald|src/test/...|~Tests + test config|mirrors main packages|JUnit classes|never in the prod artifact
violet|target/|~Generated output|classes + JAR|gitignored|wiped by mvn clean

sections.title: Complete Maven Project Directory Structure
sections.content:
```text
// Maven standard layout for order-service project
order-service/
├── pom.xml                          // Project configuration
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/                   // Production source code
│   │   │   └── com/company/order/
│   │   │       ├── OrderController.java
│   │   │       ├── OrderService.java
│   │   │       └── OrderRepository.java
│   │   └── resources/              // Config and static files
│   │       ├── application.properties
│   │       ├── data.sql           // Schema initialization
│   │       └── static/logo.png
│   └── test/
│       ├── java/                   // Test source code
│       │   └── com/company/order/
│       │       └── OrderServiceTest.java
│       └── resources/              // Test-specific configs
│           └── application-test.properties
└── target/                          // Generated output (not committed)
    ├── classes/                     // Compiled .class files
    ├── test-classes/
    └── order-service-1.0.0.jar      // Final packaged artifact
```

sections.title: When Maven's Structure Guides Your Decisions
sections.content: Follow Maven's conventions for conventional Maven Java projects unless you have a compelling reason not to — IDEs, build tools, and CI/CD pipelines expect this layout. **Spring Boot applications commonly use this structure because Spring Initializr generates it by default, and Spring Boot's auto-configuration scans src/main/resources for application.properties. **Files intended as production classpath resources normally go in `src/main/resources`, not scattered in random directories. **Static web assets** for serving HTML, CSS, or JavaScript belong in src/main/resources/static/ so Spring Boot's embedded server finds them. **Database migration scripts** for Flyway or Liquibase go in src/main/resources/db/migration/. The structure also clarifies what belongs in version control: commit everything under src/, exclude target/ in .gitignore since it's generated output. Multi-module projects nest this structure — each module is a self-contained Maven project with its own src/ and target/ directories.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Putting config files in src/main/java**: Freshers often create application.properties right next to their Java classes because that's where they're working. Resources must go in src/main/resources or they won't be included in the packaged JAR, causing "file not found" errors in production.
- **Committing the target directory to Git**: The target/ folder contains compiled bytecode and packaged JARs that are generated on every build. Freshers sometimes commit this 50MB directory, bloating the repository. Normally exclude `target/` from version control — it's reproducible build output.
- **Creating custom directories like src/code or lib/**: Fighting Maven's conventions by making up your own structure leads to hours of Maven configuration to tell it where to find things. Just follow the standard — every Java developer already knows it and Maven-aware tools understand it.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Production code:** `src/main/java`.
- **Production classpath resources:** `src/main/resources`.
- **Tests:** `src/test/java` and `src/test/resources`.
- **Build output:** `target`, normally not committed.
- **Convention, not a hard rule:** Maven can configure alternatives when a project truly needs them.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The normal Maven layout is `src/main/java` for production source, `src/main/resources` for production classpath resources, `src/test/java` for tests, and `src/test/resources` for test data. Maven puts compiled classes, reports, and packaged artifacts under `target`.

For example, a Spring Boot `application.properties` file is commonly a classpath resource under `src/main/resources`, while a deployment manifest used only by an external platform might live elsewhere. Maven plugins can configure custom directories, so the layout is not mandatory, but using the convention avoids unnecessary POM configuration and makes a new module immediately familiar.

questions.question: What is Maven Central and how does Maven use it?
questions.title: Maven Central Repository
questions.direct_answer: Maven Central is Maven's default public remote repository for many open-source Java artifacts. Maven resolves declared coordinates from configured repositories, stores downloaded artifacts in the local repository (normally `~/.m2/repository`), and reuses that cache. Not every library is in Central, and organizations often use a repository manager as a controlled proxy.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding where Java dependencies actually come from and how Maven's repository system works — fundamental for dependency troubleshooting
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Maven always downloads from the internet on every build — the local cache at tilde slash dot m2 is checked first and avoids redundant downloads
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that publishing to Maven Central requires Sonatype OSS hosting, GPG signing for security, and adherence to strict quality requirements — it's not trivial to publish there

sections.title: Maven Central: The Universal Java Library Repository
sections.content:
**Maven Central** is the standard public remote repository in Maven's default model. It contains many open-source artifacts and their POM metadata. Maven itself addresses artifacts by coordinates and can resolve from any repositories and mirrors configured by the effective POM and settings.

When an artifact is needed, Maven checks its local repository and applies update policy. If it must resolve remotely, it requests the artifact and POM from the configured remote or mirror, verifies the response according to repository policy, and stores local state for reuse. Dependencies of that artifact are then discovered from its POM.

A company often configures a repository manager as a mirror, so developers may never contact Central directly. The manager can proxy approved sources and host private artifacts. Not every artifact exists in Central, and search sites are discovery tools rather than necessarily the repository endpoint Maven downloads from.

sections.content:

sections.title: How Maven Resolves Dependencies from Maven Central
sections.content:
```text
Coordinates:
com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind:2.16.0

Repository path:
com/fasterxml/jackson/core/jackson-databind/2.16.0/
  jackson-databind-2.16.0.jar
  jackson-databind-2.16.0.pom

Default Central base URL:
https://repo.maven.apache.org/maven2/
```

Maven may request this path through a mirror configured in `settings.xml` instead of contacting Central directly.

sections.title: When Maven Central and Local Cache Matter
sections.content: Central needs no project-level repository declaration in an ordinary Maven setup because it comes from Maven's default model. Add or use another remote only when an artifact is not in Central or organizational policy requires a controlled repository. Prefer a company mirror in `settings.xml` when all builds must pass through one manager. If local state is damaged, remove only the affected artifact directory or use an appropriate dependency-plugin goal rather than treating the entire local repository as disposable by default.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming every build contacts Central:** a local artifact or configured mirror may satisfy resolution.
- **Adding Central explicitly to every POM:** normal Maven configuration already includes it.
- **Using a search website as the repository URL:** discovery pages and repository endpoints are different.
- **Deleting all of `.m2` for one bad artifact:** remove the affected path when possible; local-only installed artifacts may not be recoverable remotely.
- **Assuming every library is in Central:** internal or restricted artifacts may require an approved private repository.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Central:** Maven's standard public remote repository.
- **Coordinates:** Maven resolves group ID, artifact ID, version, and optional type/classifier.
- **Local repository:** caches resolved artifacts and metadata.
- **Effective configuration matters:** settings, mirrors, profiles, and POM repositories can change the source.
- **Company repository manager:** may proxy Central and host private artifacts.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Maven Central is the standard public remote repository used by Maven's default configuration. When a build needs coordinates that are not available locally—or a snapshot policy requires an update—Maven resolves the artifact and its POM from the configured repositories or mirror and records them in the local repository. The POM supplies metadata used to resolve transitive dependencies.

For example, `com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind:2.16.0` maps to the group path `com/fasterxml/jackson/core`, followed by the artifact and version directories. In a company, `settings.xml` often mirrors all requests through Nexus or Artifactory, so Maven may obtain the Central artifact from that internal server. Central is important, but it is neither the only repository nor contacted by every build.
